analysis.one_liner: Locks in retiree health benefits employers promised at retirement, barring later cuts or termination.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: introduced in October 1993 with no cosponsors, it was referred to a House subcommittee and died there when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the federal pension law (ERISA) so that once a worker retires with group health coverage, the employer could not later cut or terminate those benefits. Only cuts the plan spelled out in writing at retirement would be allowed. It would give retirees, unions, and fiduciaries a right to sue to stop unauthorized cuts, with courts able to issue injunctions without requiring a bond.
analysis.who_benefits: Retirees whose employers promised group health coverage at retirement but later cut or eliminated it. Roughly ten years before this bill, employers routinely reserved the right to change retiree benefits at any time, and courts often let them, leaving retirees who had worked decades for promised coverage without recourse. Unions would also gain a tool to defend members.

how_it_helps.text: Once a worker retires with group health coverage, the employer could not later terminate or reduce those benefits [S2][S3].
The only exception is for cuts the plan explicitly provided for at retirement, and only if the employer gave the retiree written notice of those terms on or before the retirement date [S2][S3].

Retirees, beneficiaries, fiduciaries, and unions could sue to block violations, and courts would grant injunctions without requiring a bond, shifting the burden to employers to prove a cut was authorized [S3].
The new rules would apply to cases already pending or filed after enactment [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that promised lifetime retiree health benefits would bear the cost of keeping those promises, potentially substantial given rising retiree medical costs and the fact that many had accounted for the ability to cut benefits. Employers would also face litigation risk and injunctions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers who promised retiree health benefits

drawbacks.text: Employers warned that locking in retiree health benefits creates open-ended liabilities, since retiree medical costs are unpredictable and employers had often structured plans assuming they could adjust benefits.
The bill could have made employers more cautious about promising retiree health coverage going forward, since they could not later trim it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A worthwhile tradeoff for retirees: it makes employer promises binding and gives retirees real remedies, but it raises employer costs and could discourage new retiree coverage.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee, then to its Labor-Management Relations subcommittee, and never advanced further before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Austin Murphy introduced the bill on October 5, 1993 [S1].
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and Labor the same day [S1][S5].
On October 22, 1993, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Labor-Management Relations, where it stayed with no further action [S5].
The bill never received a floor vote or committee vote before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who promised retiree health benefits were better off, since they retained the ability to cut or eliminate those benefits without the legal restriction this bill would have imposed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who had cut retiree benefits

for.name: Rep. Austin J. Murphy (D-PA)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to bar cuts to retiree health benefits after retirement.

against.name: House Education and Labor Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to subcommittee, where it received no further action.

sides.party_line_note: A single Democratic sponsor with no cosponsors; no recorded votes or party-line positions.

industries.industry: Large employers offering retiree health benefits
industries.note: Would have been barred from cutting or terminating retiree health benefits after retirement, facing injunctions and lawsuits if they tried. Their interest in keeping flexibility ran against retirees' interest in keeping promised coverage.
Would have gained standing to sue on behalf of members and retirees to block unauthorized benefit cuts.
